title: Changes of State
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Changes of State Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Matter changes state when heat is added or removed: melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, boiling and sublimation. The particles move faster when heated. Diagrams and flowcharts show changes of state. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 6, Quarter 1: Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Materials): solids, liquids and gases, melting and freezing, evaporation and condensation, and the particle model. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Melting, evaporation and boiling need heat.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter can change from one state to another. Heating a solid can melt it into a liquid; heating a liquid can make it evaporate or boil into a gas. Cooling a gas makes it condense into a liquid; cooling a liquid makes it freeze.

When matter is heated, its particles move faster and farther apart. During melting or boiling, the temperature stays the same until the change is complete. Changes of state are physical changes because no new substance forms.

Example

Ice cream melts in the sun. Which change of state?

Solid to liquid

Answer: melting

Example

Water droplets form on a cold glass. Which change?

Gas to liquid

Answer: condensation

Common mistakes

  • Thinking boiling and evaporation are the same.
  • Thinking condensation comes from inside the glass.
  • Thinking a change of state makes a new substance.

faq.a: Wind carries water vapor away, so evaporation is faster.

items.q: Is melted chocolate a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Melted chocolate is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.e: Solids keep their shape.

items.q: Is a glass marble a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: A glass marble is a solid.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
items.e: Water drops form on a cold glass.

items.q: Is a grain of rice a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
items.e: Puddles dry up by evaporation.

items.q: When ice melts, what happens to its mass?
items.e: Changes of state do not change mass.

items.q: Is ice a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Which property describes how easily a material bends without breaking?
items.e: Rubber is flexible.

items.q: Is chocolate (at room temperature) a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?

items.q: Is steam a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Is the bubbles in a fizzy drink a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: What happens to the particles in water when it boils?
c: They move faster and spread far apart.
items.e: Heating gives particles more energy.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: Which state of matter escapes from an open container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Why is a stainless steel pot good for cooking?
c: It conducts heat well and does not melt on the stove.
items.e: Material choice depends on properties.

items.q: Why does a metal rod expand when it is heated?

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It can be compressed easily because there is a lot of space between particles.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Why does a solid have a fixed shape?
c: Its particles do not move at all.
Strong forces hold its particles in fixed positions.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Why is a liquid hard to compress?
c: Its particles are already close together.
It has strong forces like a solid in a regular pattern.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: Why can a liquid flow?
c: Its particles can slide past one another.
It has no forces between particles.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles are far apart in a random arrangement.”

items.q: Why is a gas easy to compress?

items.q: A thermos keeps soup hot. How?
c: Its vacuum layer stops conduction and convection, and shiny walls reduce radiation.
It is made of conducting metal only.
items.e: It blocks all three kinds of heat transfer.

items.q: Carlo observes water bubbling in a pot on the stove. What happens to the motion of the particles?
items.e: Adding energy speeds particles up; removing energy slows them down.

items.q: Why are pot handles made of plastic or wood?
c: They are insulators, so they do not conduct heat to your hand.
items.e: Insulators slow heat flow.

items.q: A tight metal lid on a glass jar becomes easier to open after hot water is run over it. Which explains this?
c: The metal lid loses heat and expands.
The metal lid gains heat and expands.
The metal lid gains heat and contracts.
The metal lid loses heat and contracts.
items.e: Most things expand when they gain heat and contract when they lose heat.

items.q: The liquid in a thermometer falls when it is put in ice water. Which explains this?

items.e: Most things expand when they gain heat and contract when they lose heat.

items.q: Which way does heat flow?
c: from a cooler object to a warmer one
from a warmer object to a cooler one
items.e: Cold is not a thing that flows.
